summary: Intro demo of Redwood hosted API for chat/text gen. Covered streaming behavior, tuning common params, retry/backoff patterns, and a quick Console/Optimize tour for cost/latency suggestions. Customer interested in a trial and benchmark run; security and SSO flagged for follow-up.
transcript:
[00:00] Alyssa Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Alyssa from Redwood, today Marco and I will run through a short on-ramp for hosted chat + some best practices for streaming and retries.
[00:18] Laura Patel: Thanks Alyssa, quick context — we're building an in-app patient triage chat, latency is a big ask, and data residency is, uh, sort of a constraint.
[00:30] Marco Ruiz: Got it. We'll show the stream behavior first, then param tuning, then some console Optimize tips to keep unit costs down while meeting latency.
[00:45] James O'Neal: Quick Q, are we gonna see the streaming chunk sizes? We have trouble with partial tokens and re-renders.
[00:55] Marco Ruiz: Yeah we'll demo that; Redwood streams tokens in small chunks by default but you can control flush behavior via the streaming buffer and streaming_window settings — sometimes the transcript shows as partial words, that can be tuned.
[01:14] Priya Singh: And the SDK? We're on Python and Node.
[01:18] Alyssa Chen: We have both, we usually show Python snippets but the SDKs map 1:1. I'll paste the quickstart after the call.
[01:27] Samir Rao: Security quick flag — we need SOC2 and SAML for SSO, and KMS integration.
[01:33] Alyssa Chen: Totally. We are SOC 2 Type 2, we support SAML/SSO and customer KMS; I'll include the security whitepaper and KMS integration notes.
[01:44] [00:46] Marco Ruiz: Ok demo time. I'm going to call the chat endpoint with stream=true and a short prompt. Notice in the stream you get incremental deltas and the SDK exposes an on_message hook.
[01:02] Marco Ruiz: // (typing) // sending prompt...
[01:10] [01:10] Marco Ruiz: You can see the chunks arrive every ~40-80ms depending on model and sequence length, we show how to coalesce tokens into partial segments in the client to avoid mid-word flashes.
[01:24] James O'Neal: So flush frequency is per-token or windowed?
[01:27] Marco Ruiz: By default it's per-window; you can set streaming_window to a number of tokens or time. For low-latency single-user experiences we'd set small window and rely on prefix caching to reduce compute.
[01:40] Laura Patel: Prefix caching? can you explain that again, I've seen KV cache but prefix caching differs?
[01:46] Marco Ruiz: Right, KV cache is per-activation, prefix caching is application-level where common system prompts or static context are cached at the platform edge so you don't re-send or re-compute them, it cuts tokens billed and latency. Sometimes the transcript shows K-V as 'kay vee' in auto text.
[02:05] Priya Singh: Nice. On parameter tuning — temperature and top_p tradeoffs?
[02:09] Marco Ruiz: Yes. Temperature controls randomness, top_p controls nucleus sampling. For deterministic triage answers we recommend low temp (0–0.3) and a narrower top_p like 0.6–0.9. Max_tokens we set tight to avoid runaway usage; Console also surfaces token budget warnings.
[02:31] [02:31] Marco Ruiz: Also show the prompt template example — we demonstrate system + user split and recommended truncation strategy.
[02:39] Laura Patel: Is there server-side prompt trimming? We want to make sure we don't silently drop user context.
[02:44] Alyssa Chen: There's optional server-side truncation policy with a warn mode; you can choose strict reject/trim/warn. We'll point to that in docs.
[02:54] James O'Neal: About retries — we see transient 502s in prod, any recommended pattern?
[02:58] Marco Ruiz: Use idempotency keys for operations that can be retried safely. For streaming calls you can implement resume tokens — Redwood supports resume tokens on certain models to continue from last token if the connection drops.
[03:15] Priya Singh: Resume tokens sound ideal, how mature is that?
[03:19] Marco Ruiz: It's stable for most canonical models we ship; for custom variants we recommend benching. Marco: we'll include a resume-token example in the bench script.
[03:29] [03:30] Alyssa Chen: Quick interjection — cost vs latency: you can pick smaller model variants or quantized variants for lower cost but that increases latency sometimes, or vice versa depending on hw. Console Optimize will suggest batching and quantization profiles per workload.
[03:48] Samir Rao: For dedicated vs hosted — if we go hosted, what's SLA on latency?
[03:52] Alyssa Chen: Hosted has nominal latency profiles we publish in the catalog; Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and stricter tail latency SLA. We can map expected p50/p95 if you share traffic patterns.
[04:06] Laura Patel: We are starting small with hosted to evaluate, then consider dedicated if throughput needs grow.
[04:12] Marco Ruiz: That's common. For a pilot we recommend a sandbox project with 2–4 representative prompts and a 1k-2k request benchmark to capture p95.
[04:22] [04:22] Marco Ruiz: Now I'll flip to the Console, small tour: Optimize tab shows token breakdown, top prompts by cost, and model recommendations — e.g., switch to a quantized variant for chat-short-turns to cut cost ~30% with minimal quality loss.
[04:41] Priya Singh: Is quantization transparent? Any quality checks?
[04:44] Marco Ruiz: Optimize has guardrails — it will run a quick eval on your prompt set and show expected delta in BLEU-ish or custom scoring; you can pin quality thresholds before auto-applying.
[04:58] James O'Neal: Any hard limits on requests/sec for hosted? We expect bursts during morning triage.
[05:03] Alyssa Chen: There's soft rate limits per account, and we support burst policies; for sustained high QPS we recommend Dedicated. We'll show how to request bursts via the console and set autoscale rules.
[05:18] Samir Rao: KMS — are we able to use our HSM?
[05:21] Alyssa Chen: Yes, Redwood supports customer-managed keys and HSM integrations depending on the plan — I'll share the KMS integration doc.
[05:30] [05:30] Marco Ruiz: Back to errors: typical pattern is exponential backoff with jitter for transient server errors, and immediate failover to lower-cost fallback model for latency-sensitive requests. We demo fallback policy in the console.
[05:46] Laura Patel: Can fallback cause hallucinations because model changes?
[05:50] Marco Ruiz: Good point. Rollouts can map to compatible model variants and you can define semantic compatibility rules; Optimize also surfaces quality regressions if fallback causes divergence.
[06:04] Priya Singh: Any live example of retries with resume token?
[06:08] Marco Ruiz: Yes — I'm re-running a short prompt, will kill the stream at token ~12 to show resume.
[06:16] [06:16] Marco Ruiz: // kills connection // reconnecting...
[06:22] Marco Ruiz: See it resumed from resume_token=abc123 and the client stitched seamlessly. There's small duplication window you can dedupe on the client.
[06:33] James O'Neal: That's promising.
[06:35] [06:35] Priya Singh: Any gotchas with streaming on mobile clients?
[06:38] Marco Ruiz: Mobile networks are flaky — prefer shorter streaming windows and client-side aggregation. Also use heartbeat pings to detect disconnects earlier.
[06:49] Alyssa Chen: Quick commercial note — trial includes credits and a seat in our onboarding channel; we can set a two-week bench window.
[06:58] Laura Patel: Security review will want penetration test reports and data retention policy.
[07:04] Alyssa Chen: We'll send SOC2 and data retention doc; retention is configurable per workspace.
[07:11] Samir Rao: Do you log raw prompts by default?
[07:15] Marco Ruiz: No, logs are redact-by-default for PII; you can toggle detailed logging for troubleshooting with audit trails enabled.
[07:24] [07:24] James O'Neal: For benching, can we get per-token latency breakdowns?
[07:28] Marco Ruiz: Yes, Console traces show token-level timing, KV cache hits, and network overhead. We'll include an example CSV export.
[07:40] Priya Singh: One last question — how to avoid token explosion with long histories?
[07:44] Marco Ruiz: Use summary compression, rolling context windows, and relevance-based pruning. Optimize can suggest retention policies per route.
[07:57] Alyssa Chen: Ok final recap: Alyssa will send pricing, security docs, recording, and trial link. Marco will prepare the bench scripts and resume-token examples. Customer will provide sample prompts and latency targets.
[08:14] Laura Patel: Sounds good, thanks both.
[08:16] Alyssa Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the items.
[08:20] [08:20] (call ends)

Notes about transcription: occasional auto-caps and speaker mislabels present (e.g., Speaker 1), some technical terms rendered phonetically ("K-V cache" vs "KV cache").
